column1: # The settings of the startup screen (LauncherActivity) and the in-game menu (vk/overlay.cpp): one row each, tab-separated:
#   key  tab  flags  default  values  names  label  help  needs
# key: the environment variable the game reads (launch.env); @name: a row that opens a page instead of holding a value;
#   =: a section heading (flag H), which shows only its label.
# values / names: '|'-separated, in the same order. Rows show in file order; tabs in order of first appearance.
# flags: L applies at once in the game (the rest are saved for the next start), Q also in the quick menu, X experimental,
#   D only when the app carries Turnip, S startup screen only, P opens a page (@ rows), H a section heading.
# Values starting with lsfg show only once the startup screen has made LSFG's shaders (Lsfg.java, vk/overlay.cpp).
# needs (optional): KEY=value|value: the row shows only while that setting has one of these values. A section must start
#   with a row that always shows. Help: one or two plain sentences, what it does and the trade-off; no figures that age.

column8: Runs the game as a handheld or as if docked to a TV. Docked draws more detail but works the GPU harder.

How detailed the 3D world is before it is fitted to the screen. Original is the Switch’s own. Lower runs cooler but looks softer; sizes above the screen look smoother but cost far more GPU power and memory.

column6: FSR 1 · Balanced|NIS · Crisp|SGSR · Sharp|CAS · Sharpened|Lanczos · Detailed|Bicubic · Smooth|Bilinear · Soft|Nearest · Pixelated|MMPX · Retro|Super-xBR · Painted|ScaleFX · Cartoon
column8: How the picture is enlarged to fill the screen. FSR 1, NIS, SGSR and CAS sharpen; Lanczos, Bicubic and Bilinear go from crisp to soft; Nearest shows the pixels; MMPX, Super-xBR and ScaleFX give a flat, painted look. Unused when the picture already fills the screen.
How crisp FSR 1 makes the picture. Stronger looks more detailed but makes jagged edges stand out; Off adds no sharpening.
How large ScaleFX draws before the picture is fitted to the screen. Screen size suits most screens and costs least; 2× and 3× cost more GPU time.

Smooths jagged edges in the world; the HUD stays sharp. SMAA suits most players. SMAA T2x also calms flicker on distant edges but can trail in fast motion. TAA blends several frames for the calmest, slightly softer picture. T2x and TAA need docked mode; in handheld they act like SMAA.
How much TAA smooths the picture. Sharp keeps the most detail but lets a little shimmer through; Soft is the calmest.

How the game enlarges its picture to the screen when docked. The game’s own filter sharpens, so edges can crawl as the camera moves; Neutral adds no sharpening; Soft and Softer blur slightly for a calmer look.
How hard SMAA looks for edges. High is enough for most scenes; Ultra catches fainter edges for a little more GPU time.
Builds each frame from several smaller ones in place of SMAA, smoothing distant edges further. Lights can shimmer and fast characters smear, and it costs a lot of GPU time.
Keeps the ground and walls sharp when seen at a shallow angle. Higher looks sharper for a little GPU time.
How sharp the sun’s shadows are, especially leaves on the ground. Higher costs very little.
How far away the sun casts shadows. Medium and Near drop the shadows of distant hills and trees for a little less GPU work; nearby shadows stay.
The most pictures shown each second, counting generated ones. A lower limit saves power and heat. The game always runs at normal speed.
How often the screen updates. 120 Hz looks smoother when the frame rate is uneven; 60 Hz saves power. Some devices drop to 60 Hz on their own when very hot.

Adds pictures between the ones the game draws for smoother motion, with a little more input delay. Homemade is the lightest; FSR 3.1 always doubles; LSFG often looks cleanest but costs the most and needs your Lossless.dll (Tools › Lossless Scaling on the startup screen). Generation pauses if heat drops the screen to 60 Hz.
How many pictures are added. Fill adds one only when the game misses the frame rate limit; ×2 holds the game to half the limit and adds one after every frame.

How many pictures LSFG adds. Fill adds them only when the game misses the limit. ×1.5 to ×4 hold the game to the limit divided by that number: higher gives the game more time per frame but shows more errors in fast motion.
How the game’s HUD looks with frame generation. Real frames stays sharp but moves at the game’s own rate; Generated moves smoothly, but moving text can smear.
How closely LSFG follows motion. Lower uses less GPU time, but fast motion looks blurrier.
A lighter version of LSFG: less GPU time, slightly more visual errors.
Up to the limit lets the game run as fast as the frame rate limit allows. Original keeps the Switch’s 30 to 40 frames per second.
Gives every game frame the same time on screen: steadier, but with more input delay. Frame generation paces its own pictures either way.
Choose which button does each action, such as jump or attack. Menus follow the Face buttons setting instead.
How A, B, X and Y match the Switch’s. By position puts A on the right, as on a Switch; By label uses the letter printed on each button.
Which button symbols the game’s prompts show. Only the pictures change, never what a button does.
Aim by tilting the device, like the gyro controls on a Switch.
The game’s volume. The game is muted while this menu is open.
The frame rate, counting every picture shown; with frame generation, also how many are real. “Low” is the 1% low of the last 512 game frames (about 17 s at 30 fps), so a stutter stays in it a while.
How long each game frame takes, with a graph of the last few seconds. The faint line is the frame rate limit; the graph turns red where a frame ran long.
How busy the CPU and GPU are, and the GPU’s speed. The CPU figure weighs each core by its speed; the busiest core is shown too, since one busy core can hold the game back.
How much power the device draws, the CPU and GPU temperatures, and the fan speed where the device reports one.
How long frame generation spends on each picture, and how long a finished picture waits to reach the screen. A longer wait means more input delay.
The upscaler, anti-aliasing, frame generation and frame rate limit in use: handy for comparing screenshots and recordings.
How often the screen is updating right now. Some devices drop to 60 Hz when very hot.
How many shaders are being built right now. A stutter while this is above zero is a shader being built.
The graphics driver in use and its version.
Which corner of the screen the performance overlay sits in.
How large the performance overlay’s text and graph are.
How dark the panel behind the performance overlay is. Less shows more of the game; more keeps the text readable over bright scenes.
The graphics driver the game uses: your device’s own, the bundled Turnip driver for Adreno GPUs, or one from a .zip made for emulators. Each keeps its own shader cache.
Tells Android how long each frame takes, so it raises the CPU speed only as far as needed, saving power and heat.
Keeps a video of the last 30 seconds so a bug report can include it, even after a crash. Uses about 45 MB of storage and a little GPU time.
